entries.title: Albrecht Dürer on Extracting Art from the Natural World
entries.body_text: For in truth, art is embedded in nature; he who can extract it, has it.
entries.image_alt_text: Young Hare by Albrecht Dürer, 1502, watercolor and gouache on paper, 25.1 x 22.6 cm, Albertina Museum, Vienna
entries.source_name: Dürer, Albrecht. 'Vier Bücher von menschlicher Proportion' (Four Books on Human Proportion). Nuremberg, 1528.
entries.rights_note: Public domain. Albrecht Dürer died April 6, 1528; 'Young Hare' created 1502. Image sourced from Wikimedia Commons.

entries.title: Auguste Rodin: Making the Process the Subject
entries.body_text: Auguste Rodin was born on November 12, 1840, in Paris. Three times rejected by the École des Beaux-Arts, he spent years as a decorative craftsman before his monumental bronze 'The Age of Bronze' (1877) launched his reputation — and an accusation that he had cast it from a live model, so convincingly real was its surface. Rodin's great achievement was making the working process itself legible in the finished sculpture: unresolved surfaces, patches of raw plaster, figures emerging unfinished from rough stone. He received the commission for 'The Gates of Hell' in 1880 — a monumental portal depicting Dante's Inferno — and never stopped revising it, producing from its figures more than 200 individual sculptures including 'The Thinker,' 'The Kiss,' and 'The Three Shades.' His studio in Meudon, south of Paris, where he worked through the long grey autumns of his later years, is now a museum housing his plaster casts, marbles, and bronzes. Rodin died there on November 17, 1917, just five days after his 77th birthday.
entries.image_alt_text: The Thinker by Auguste Rodin, 1902, bronze, 186 x 98 x 140 cm, Musée Rodin, Paris
entries.rights_note: Auguste Rodin died November 17, 1917. The original sculpture is in the public domain. Photograph sourced from Wikimedia Commons under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike license.

entries.title: Sonia Delaunay: When the Canvas Became Cloth
entries.body_text: Sonia Delaunay was born Sophie Stern on November 14, 1885, in Hradyzk, Ukraine, then part of the Russian Empire. Adopted by a wealthy uncle in St. Petersburg, she studied art in Karlsruhe and Paris before settling permanently in France. In 1910 she married Robert Delaunay and together they developed Simultanism — a theory of pure abstraction based on the optical dynamism of contrasting color pairs — that Robert would later name Orphism. But where Robert confined himself to canvas, Sonia applied Simultanism to every surface that came to hand: bookbinding, costume, ceramics, furniture, and above all textile and fashion design. Her 1913 'Simultaneous Dress' — a patchwork garment she made for herself from contrasting fabric swatches — was one of the first statements of wearable art in the 20th century. At the 1925 Paris International Exhibition she ran a Simultanism boutique and sold fabrics to Coco Chanel. Her geometric textile designs, in their harvest palettes of amber, rust, gold, and cobalt, remain among the most influential works of applied modernism. In 1964, she became the first living woman artist to hold a retrospective at the Louvre. She died on December 5, 1979.
entries.image_alt_text: Electric Prisms by Sonia Delaunay, 1914, oil on canvas, 250 x 250 cm, Centre Georges Pompidou, Paris
entries.source_name: Centre Georges Pompidou, Paris / Wikimedia Commons
entries.rights_note: 'Electric Prisms' (1914) was first publicly exhibited before January 1, 1928, and is in the public domain in the United States. Sonia Delaunay died December 5, 1979; later works remain under copyright in France and the EU. Image sourced from Wikimedia Commons.

entries.title: Faith Ringgold on Making the Art Only You Can Make
entries.body_text: I am an artist. And I am a woman. And I am Black. And my art reflects all of those things.
entries.image_alt_text: Tar Beach by Faith Ringgold, 1988, acrylic on canvas, bordered with printed, painted, quilted, and pieced cloth, 188.9 x 174 cm, Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York
entries.source_name: Ringgold, Faith. 'We Flew Over the Bridge: The Memoirs of Faith Ringgold.' Little, Brown, 1995; widely cited in Guggenheim Museum and Whitney Museum exhibition texts.
entries.rights_note: Faith Ringgold died April 12, 2024. Works are under copyright administered by the Faith Ringgold Estate / ACA Galleries. Image URL withheld.

entries.title: Charles White on Art as Liberation
entries.body_text: Art must be an integral part of the struggle. It can't simply mirror what is taking place. It must ally itself with the forces of liberation.
entries.image_alt_text: Harvest Talk by Charles White, 1953, lithograph on paper, depicting two Black figures in conversation against a warm autumn landscape
entries.source_name: Widely attributed to Charles White; cited in the Charles White retrospective catalogue, Art Institute of Chicago / Museum of Modern Art, 2018.
entries.rights_note: Charles White died October 3, 1979. Works are under copyright administered by the Charles White Art Trust / Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York. Image URL withheld.

entries.title: Gordon Parks: Camera as Weapon, Witness, and Mirror
entries.body_text: Gordon Parks was born on November 30, 1912, in Fort Scott, Kansas — the youngest of fifteen children in a family he described as poor but never defeated. Largely self-taught, Parks purchased his first camera at a pawnshop for $7.50. In 1942 he joined the Farm Security Administration (FSA) under Roy Stryker, and on his first day in Washington, D.C., photographed Ella Watson, a Black government cleaning woman, holding her mop in front of an American flag. The resulting image — 'American Gothic, Washington, D.C.' — placed the gap between American ideals and American reality into a single, unforgettable frame. Parks joined LIFE magazine in 1948 as its first Black staff photographer, documenting segregation, poverty, fashion, and celebrity across four decades. He was also a novelist, poet, composer, and filmmaker: his 1971 film 'Shaft' made him the first Black director of a major Hollywood studio production. He died on March 7, 2006, in New York. His life's work is a refusal to let any single medium contain the full scope of what he had witnessed and what he knew.
entries.image_alt_text: American Gothic, Washington, D.C. by Gordon Parks, 1942, gelatin silver print, depicting Ella Watson, a Black government cleaning woman, standing before an American flag with a mop and broom
